Obdurate

/AHB-dur-it/ — emphasis on first syllable · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Someone who is obdurate stubbornly refuses to change their mind or behavior, even when others try to persuade them.

The obdurate landlord refused every offer, no matter how generous.

Worked Example

After his friends explained the dangers in detail, the obdurate driver ignored every warning and drove recklessly across town.

Obdurate is more precise than 'stubborn' because it emphasizes not just resistance to change, but the active refusal to be persuaded despite others' efforts. The stubbornness here is specifically about ignoring appeals — that's what obdurate names.

How Obdurate Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

stubborn

stubborn: refusing to change despite reasonable arguments

inflexible

inflexible: rigidly unwilling to adapt or bend

intransigent

intransigent: flatly refusing any compromise at all

Antonyms

amenable

amenable: willing to cooperate and be persuaded

yielding

yielding: giving way readily to others' wishes

How Strong Is It? — resistant → stubborn → obdurate → immovable

resistant vs. obdurate

resistant vs. obdurate: Resistant is milder than obdurate: a resistant person pushes back at first, while an obdurate person has hardened against all persuasion.

stubborn vs. obdurate

stubborn vs. obdurate: Stubborn is strong, but obdurate goes further — a stubborn person digs in, while an obdurate one has hardened so completely that no appeal can reach them.

immovable vs. obdurate

immovable vs. obdurate: Immovable is stronger even than obdurate: an obdurate person stubbornly refuses to soften, but an immovable one is as fixed as stone, beyond any hope of change.

Sort It Out

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — ob-

Prefix — ob-: against (Latin)

Root — dur

Root — dur: hard (from durus, 'hard') (Latin)

Suffix — -ate

Suffix — -ate: having the quality of (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Obdurate literally means 'hardened against' — ob- ('against') plus durus ('hard'). Someone obdurate has hardened their heart against every plea, stubbornly refusing to change their mind no matter what.

Use the root in a new word: durable

Use the root in a new word: durable: A durable backpack is hard to wear out — the same Latin root durus, 'hard,' that makes an obdurate person hard to persuade.

Root Check

Word Choice

formal / literary

Obdurate is stronger and more formal than 'stubborn.' Use it when you want to emphasize that someone has hardened themselves against others' attempts to persuade them — there's an almost willful resistance. For simple stubbornness without that layer of defiance, 'stubborn' is the plainer word.
